**Surah al-Qamar is Meccan, and it has fifty-five verses.**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ ﴿They denied and followed their desires, and every matter will be settled.﴾ ﴿There had certainly come to them of the news that which contained a deterrent.﴾ ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings did not avail.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them. The day the caller calls to a terrible thing,﴾ ﴿with eyes humbled, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:7) ﴿Hastening toward the caller, the disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:8) ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and they denied Our servant and said, "He is a madman," and he was rebuked.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:9) ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overpowered, so help me."﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:10) ﴿So We opened the gates of the heaven with water pouring forth.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:11) ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:12) ﴿And We carried him on a vessel of planks and nails,﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:13) ﴿sailing under Our eyes, as a reward for one who had been denied.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:14) ﴿And We left it as a sign. Is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:15) ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:16) ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance. Is there anyone who will remember?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:17)

.

(p-172) Al-jadath: the grave. Its th (ث) may be changed to f (ف), so it is said jadaf, just as they changed thumma (ثُمَّ) to fumma (فُمَّ). The water poured forth (infahara al-ma'): it descended with force and abundance. The poet said:

*"The east wind turned it, then there passed over it a heavy downpour from the south, pouring forth."*

Al-dusur: the nails with which the ship is fastened. Its singular is dissar, like kitab and kutub. It is said: "I fastened the ship" (dasartu al-safina) when I secured it with nails. Al-Layth and the author of al-Sihah said: al-dusur are cords with which the planks of the ship are tied. Al-sarsar: that which is severe in sound or in cold. It is either from the screech (sarir) of a door, which is its sound, or from al-sirr, which is cold. It is an原 root built on the pattern fa'lal according to the majority of scholars. Al-'ajuz: the back part of a thing. Al-munqa'ir: that which is uprooted from its base. "I uprooted the tree" (qa'artu al-shajarata qa'ran) means I pulled it from its root, and it became uprooted (infaqara). For a well: "I descended until I reached its bottom." For a vessel: "I drank what was in it until I reached its bottom." "I made its well deep" (aqra'tuhu al-bi'r) means I made a bottom for it. Al-ashir: the insolent. It has been read ashira with a kasra, yash'aru ashaaran, so he is ashir, ashir, and ashran, and the people are ushara, like sakran and sukara. Saqar: a proper name for Hell, derived from saqarat-hu al-nar (the fire scorched him) with a sin, or from saqartu-hu with a sad when you blackened him. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"When the sun melts, he shields himself from its scorching heat with the branches of a tree of mixed shade, in a sandhill grown dense."*

Saqar is not declined (did not take tanwin) because it is a proper noun and feminine. The vowel of its middle letter is treated as if it were the fourth letter, as in Zaynab.

Is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:15) ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:16) ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance. Is there anyone who will remember?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:17) .

(p-173) This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars (al-jumhur). It was also said that it was revealed on the Day of Badr. Muqatil said: it is Meccan except for three verses. The first is ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united force, victorious"?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:44), and the last is ﴿more calamitous and bitter﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:46).

The occasion of its revelation was that the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Messenger (ﷺ), "If you are truthful, split the moon for us into two halves," and they promised him belief if he did so. This was the night of Badr. He asked his Lord, and the moon split, one half upon al-Safa and one half upon Qay'qa'an. The people of Makkah said, "This is a heavenly sign that magic cannot affect." Abu Jahl said, "Wait until the people of the deserts come to us. If they report its splitting, then it is true; otherwise, Muhammad has bewitched our eyes." They came and reported the splitting of the moon, so Abu Jahl turned away and said, ﴿Continuous magic﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:2).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the moon was split into two pieces, one piece over al-Suwayda' and one piece over al-Hudaybiyah. And from him: the moon split twice in Makkah. And from him: it split into two halves, one half that departed and one half that remained.

The connection of the beginning of the surah to the end of what precedes it is evident. He said, ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾ (al-Najm 53:57), and He said, ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾. Among those who witnessed the splitting of the moon were Ibn Mas'ud and Jubayr ibn Mut'im. Ibn 'Umar, Anas, Hudhayfah, and Ibn 'Abbas reported it. "When Allah showed the people the splitting of the moon, the Messenger (ﷺ) said, 'Bear witness.'" The polytheists said at that time, "Muhammad has bewitched us," and some of them said, "He has bewitched the moon."

The Ummah is in agreement against the view of the one who claimed that His saying ﴿and the moon has split﴾ means that it will split on the Day of Resurrection. What refutes this from the verse is His saying ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ Therefore, this statement would not fit unless it came after the manifestation of what they had specifically asked for, namely the splitting of the moon.

It was also said: they asked for a sign in general, so He showed them this heavenly sign, which is among the greatest signs, and this is an effect in the upper world. Hudhayfah recited: "and the moon has split" (wa qad inshaqqa al-qamar), meaning "has drawn near." The splitting of the moon is among the signs of its drawing near, just as you say, "The emir has come, and the one bringing good news of his arrival has come." Hudhayfah delivered a sermon in al-Mada'in and then said, "Indeed the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split in the time of your Prophet."

There is no consideration given to the statement of al-Hasan that the meaning is: when the Hour comes, the moon will split after the second blast. Nor is there consideration given to the view of one who said that its splitting is an expression for the splitting of darkness when it rises through it, so the meaning is: the matter became manifest. The Arabs use the moon as an example of what is clear, just as dawn is called falaq at the splitting of darkness from it, and splitting may be expressed by the word for cleaving. Al-Nabighah said:

*"When they turned their backs, and there was a clamor among them, a caller called to us at the splitting of the dawn."*

These are corrupt statements, and were it not that the commentators mentioned them, I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely.

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. It has been read as yurawa (passive), meaning: it is their nature and state that whenever they see what indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) of the dazzling signs, they turn away from believing in him and in that sign. The sentence came in conditional form to show that in the future they will be in a state like their state in the past, and they will say: ﴿Continuous magic﴾, meaning: lasting. From this is the saying of the poet:

(p-174) *"Indeed, the world is only nights and days, and nothing upright remains lasting."*

That is, nothing lasting. When they saw the signs following one another without interruption, they said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Akhfash said: mustamirr means tightly bound, firmly fastened with the strands of a rope, meaning: magic that has been made firm. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Until his bitter firmness was established upon a secret, sincere in resolve, neither softened nor weakened."*

Anas, Yaman, Mujahid, al-Kisa'i, and al-Farra' said, and al-Nahhas chose this: mustamirr means passing and departing, quickly ceasing. They reasoned by this to console themselves. It was also said: mustamirr means extremely bitter, that is, something that we find loathsome and bitter. It is said: "the thing became bitter" (marra al-shay'u wa amarra) when it became bitter, and "he made it bitter" (amarra ghayrahu wa marrahu) when he made something else bitter, and it is both intransitive and transitive. It was also said: mustamirr means that one part resembles another, that is, its actions continued in this manner of imaginings. It was also said: mustamirr means passing from the earth to the sky, that is, his magic reached the point that he bewitched the moon.

﴿And they denied﴾: that is, the signs and the one who brought them. That is, they said, "This is continuous magic; Muhammad has bewitched us."

﴿And followed their desires﴾: that is, the lusts of their souls and what they craved.

﴿Wa kullu amrin mustaqirr﴾: read with a kasra on the qaf and a damma on the ra'. It may be the subject (mubtada') or the predicate (khabar). Muqatil said: it has an end to which it arrives. Al-Kalbi said: it has a reality (haqiqa) that it settles into. Whatever is in this world will become manifest, and whatever is in the Hereafter will be known. Qatadah said: its meaning is that good settles upon the people of good and evil upon the people of evil. It has also been said: the truth settles, manifest and firm, and falsehood is destroyed and gone. It has also been said: every matter of theirs and of His settles into humiliation or victory in this world, and into happiness or misery in the Hereafter.

Shaybah recited mustaqarr with a fatha on the qaf, and it is reported from Nafi'. Abu Hatim said: there is no basis for a fatha on the qaf. End of quotation. It has been explained as the omission of a modifier, meaning "possessing settledness" or "a time of settledness."

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Ali recited mustaqirrin with a kasra on both the qaf and the ra', as an attribute (sifah) of amr.

Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning that wa kullu is conjoined (ma'tuf) to al-sa'ah, so that the sense is: "The Hour has drawn near, and every settled matter has drawn near, settling and its state becoming clear." This is far-fetched, because of the long separation by three clauses, and it is far-fetched that such a construction would occur in Arabic speech, as in the example: "I ate bread, and I struck Zayd, and if Zayd comes, I honor him, and he traveled to the people of so-and-so, and meat," so that "and meat" would be conjoined to "bread." Indeed, nothing like it is found in the speech of the Arabs.

The author of al-Lawami' explained it as the predicate of kull, so it is nominative (marfu') in origin, but it is put in the genitive (majrur) by proximity (lil-mujawarah). This is not sound, because genitive by proximity is an extreme anomaly (ghayat al-shudhudh), and because it is not attested in the predicate of a subject; it is attested only in the attribute, though grammarians disagree about its occurrence. The easier view is that the predicate is omitted, its meaning being indicated by context, and the estimate is: ﴿wa kullu amrin mustaqirrun﴾ bali'uhu, "will reach them," because before it is ﴿and they denied and followed their desires﴾. That is: "And every matter is settled for them by decree, good or evil, and they will reach it." It has also been said: the predicate is "a far-reaching wisdom" (hikmah baligha), meaning: "And every matter that is settled is a far-reaching wisdom." In that case ﴿And there has already come to them of the reports that which contains a deterrent﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) between the subject and its predicate.

﴿Wa laqad ja'ahum mina al-anba'﴾: that is, of the reports contained in the Qur'an concerning the destruction of those who denied the prophets, and what they will come to in the Hereafter.

﴿ma fihi muzdajar﴾: that is, a restraining deterrence (izdijar radi') for them from what they are in, or a place of deterrence and restraint; that is, that is a place of deterrence, or a likely cause of it.

It has been read as muzzajar, by replacing the t of the infi'al form with z and assimilating the z into it. Zayd ibn Ali recited muzjir, an active participle of azjara, meaning "one who has a deterrent," like a'shaba, "one who has grass." The majority read ﴿hikmatun baligha﴾ with both in the nominative. They permitted that hikmah be a substitute (badal) for muzdajar or for ma, or the predicate of an omitted subject. The opinion of one who made it the predicate of kull in the reading of one who recited "mustaqirr" in the genitive has already been mentioned. Al-Yamani recited hikmatan baligatan with both in the accusative, as a circumstantial (hal) of ma, whether ma is a relative pronoun or an indefinite noun specified by its attribute. Hikmah is described as baligha because it reaches (tablughu) other things.

﴿Fa ma tughni al-nudhur﴾: with these disbelievers.

Then He consoled His Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them, for warning is of no benefit among them.

Then He mentioned some of the states of the Hereafter and what they will come to, since that is connected to the drawing near of the Hour, saying: ﴿On the day when the caller calls﴾. The word yawm is governed by an implied verb, "remember," as said by al-Rummani, or by "they will come forth." Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "turn away from them until a day," but this is weak both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. As for wording, it omits ila ("until"). As for meaning, his turning away from them is not specifically tied to ﴿the day when the caller calls﴾.

They permitted that it be governed by His saying ﴿Fa ma tughni al-nudhur﴾, with ﴿So turn away from them﴾ being a parenthetical clause. It may also be governed by His saying ﴿The disbelievers will say﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]; governed by an implied "wait"; governed by His saying ﴿So turn away﴾, though this is very weak; or governed by mustaqirr, which is also far-fetched.

The waw in yad'u was omitted from the orthography (rasm) following the pronunciation, and the ya' in al-da'i was dropped for lightness, treating the definite article al- as a substitute for what replaces it, which is tanwin. Just as it is dropped with tanwin, it is dropped with al-. The caller (al-da'i) is Israfil, or Jibril, or another angel appointed for that task; there are several opinions.

It has also been said: the truth settles, manifest and firm, and falsehood is destroyed and gone. It has also been said: every matter of theirs and of His settles into humiliation or victory in this world, and into happiness or misery in the Hereafter.

Shaybah recited mustaqarr with a fatha on the qaf, and it is reported from Nafi'. Abu Hatim said: there is no basis for a fatha on the qaf. End of quotation. It has been explained as the omission of a modifier, meaning "possessing settledness" or "a time of settledness."

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Ali recited mustaqirrin with a kasra on both the qaf and the ra', as an attribute (sifah) of amr.

Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning that wa kullu is conjoined (ma'tuf) to al-sa'ah, so that the sense is: "The Hour has drawn near, and every settled matter has drawn near, settling and its state becoming clear." This is far-fetched, because of the long separation by three clauses, and it is far-fetched that such a construction would occur in Arabic speech, as in the example: "I ate bread, and I struck Zayd, and if Zayd comes, I honor him, and he traveled to the people of so-and-so, and meat," so that "and meat" would be conjoined to "bread." Indeed, nothing like it is found in the speech of the Arabs.

The author of al-Lawami' explained it as the predicate of kull, so it is nominative (marfu') in origin, but it is put in the genitive (majrur) by proximity (lil-mujawarah). This is not sound, because genitive by proximity is an extreme anomaly (ghayat al-shudhudh), and because it is not attested in the predicate of a subject; it is attested only in the attribute, though grammarians disagree about its occurrence. That is: "And every matter is settled for them by decree, good or evil, and they will reach it." It has also been said: the predicate is "a far-reaching wisdom" (hikmah baligha), meaning: "And every matter that is settled is a far-reaching wisdom." **Surah al-Qamar is Meccan, and it has fifty-five verses.**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This was the night of Badr. He asked his Lord, and the moon split, one half upon al-Safa and one half upon Qay'qa'an. The people of Makkah said, "This is a heavenly sign that magic cannot affect." Abu Jahl said, "Wait until the people of the deserts come to us. If they report its splitting, then it is true; otherwise, Muhammad has bewitched our eyes." They came and reported the splitting of the moon, so Abu Jahl turned away and said, ﴿Continuous magic﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:2).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the moon was split into two pieces, one piece over al-Suwayda' and one piece over al-Hudaybiyah. And from him: the moon split twice in Makkah. And from him: it split into two halves, one half that departed and one half that remained.

"When Allah showed the people the splitting of the moon, the Messenger (ﷺ) said, 'Bear witness.'" The polytheists said at that time, "Muhammad has bewitched us," and some of them said, "He has bewitched the moon."

What refutes this from the verse is His saying ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ Therefore, this statement would not fit unless it came after the manifestation of what they had specifically asked for, namely the splitting of the moon.

It was also said: they asked for a sign in general, so He showed them this heavenly sign, which is among the greatest signs, and this is an effect in the upper world. Hudhayfah recited: "and the moon has split" (wa qad inshaqqa al-qamar), meaning "has drawn near." The splitting of the moon is among the signs of its drawing near, just as you say, "The emir has come, and the one bringing good news of his arrival has come." Hudhayfah delivered a sermon in al-Mada'in and then said, "Indeed the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split in the time of your Prophet."

There is no consideration given to the statement of al-Hasan that the meaning is: when the Hour comes, the moon will split after the second blast. Nor is there consideration given to the view of one who said that its splitting is an expression for the splitting of darkness when it rises through it, so the meaning is: the matter became manifest. The Arabs use the moon as an example of what is clear, just as dawn is called falaq at the splitting of darkness from it, and splitting may be expressed by the word for cleaving. Al-Nabighah said:

*"When they turned their backs, and there was a clamor among them, a caller called to us at the splitting of the dawn."*

These are corrupt statements, and were it not that the commentators mentioned them, I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely.

The sentence came in conditional form to show that in the future they will be in a state like their state in the past, and they will say: ﴿Continuous magic﴾, meaning: lasting. From this is the saying of the poet:

That is, nothing lasting. When they saw the signs following one another without interruption, they said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Akhfash said: mustamirr means tightly bound, firmly fastened with the strands of a rope, meaning: magic that has been made firm. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Until his bitter firmness was established upon a secret, sincere in resolve, neither softened nor weakened."*

Anas, Yaman, Mujahid, al-Kisa'i, and al-Farra' said, and al-Nahhas chose this: mustamirr means passing and departing, quickly ceasing. They reasoned by this to console themselves. It was also said: mustamirr means extremely bitter, that is, something that we find loathsome and bitter. It is said: "the thing became bitter" (marra al-shay'u wa amarra) when it became bitter, and "he made it bitter" (amarra ghayrahu wa marrahu) when he made something else bitter, and it is both intransitive and transitive. It was also said: mustamirr means that one part resembles another, that is, its actions continued in this manner of imaginings. It was also said: mustamirr means passing from the earth to the sky, that is, his magic reached the point that he bewitched the moon.

The occasion of its revelation was that the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Messenger (ﷺ), "If you are truthful, split the moon for us into two halves," and they promised him belief if he did so. This was the night of Badr. He asked his Lord, and the moon split, one half upon al-Safa and one half upon Qay'qa'an. The people of Makkah said, "This is a heavenly sign that magic cannot affect." Abu Jahl said, "Wait until the people of the deserts come to us. If they report its splitting, then it is true; otherwise, Muhammad has bewitched our eyes." They came and reported the splitting of the moon, so Abu Jahl turned away and said, ﴿Continuous magic﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:2).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the moon was split into two pieces, one piece over al-Suwayda' and one piece over al-Hudaybiyah. And from him: the moon split twice in Makkah. And from him: it split into two halves, one half that departed and one half that remained.

The connection of the beginning of the surah to the end of what precedes it is evident. He said, ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾ (al-Najm 53:57), and He said, ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾. Among those who witnessed the splitting of the moon were Ibn Mas'ud and Jubayr ibn Mut'im. Ibn 'Umar, Anas, Hudhayfah, and Ibn 'Abbas reported it. "When Allah showed the people the splitting of the moon, the Messenger (ﷺ) said, 'Bear witness.'" The polytheists said at that time, "Muhammad has bewitched us," and some of them said, "He has bewitched the moon."

The Ummah is in agreement against the view of the one who claimed that His saying ﴿and the moon has split﴾ means that it will split on the Day of Resurrection. What refutes this from the verse is His saying ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ Therefore, this statement would not fit unless it came after the manifestation of what they had specifically asked for, namely the splitting of the moon.

It was also said: they asked for a sign in general, so He showed them this heavenly sign, which is among the greatest signs, and this is an effect in the upper world. Hudhayfah recited: "and the moon has split" (wa qad inshaqqa al-qamar), meaning "has drawn near." The splitting of the moon is among the signs of its drawing near, just as you say, "The emir has come, and the one bringing good news of his arrival has come." Hudhayfah delivered a sermon in al-Mada'in and then said, "Indeed the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split in the time of your Prophet."

There is no consideration given to the statement of al-Hasan that the meaning is: when the Hour comes, the moon will split after the second blast. Nor is there consideration given to the view of one who said that its splitting is an expression for the splitting of darkness when it rises through it, so the meaning is: the matter became manifest. The Arabs use the moon as an example of what is clear, just as dawn is called falaq at the splitting of darkness from it, and splitting may be expressed by the word for cleaving. Al-Nabighah said:

*"When they turned their backs, and there was a clamor among them, a caller called to us at the splitting of the dawn."*

These are corrupt statements, and were it not that the commentators mentioned them, I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely.

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. It has been read as yurawa (passive), meaning: it is their nature and state that whenever they see what indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) of the dazzling signs, they turn away from believing in him and in that sign. The sentence came in conditional form to show that in the future they will be in a state like their state in the past, and they will say: ﴿Continuous magic﴾, meaning: lasting. From this is the saying of the poet:

(p-174) *"Indeed, the world is only nights and days, and nothing upright remains lasting."*

That is, nothing lasting. When they saw the signs following one another without interruption, they said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Akhfash said: mustamirr means tightly bound, firmly fastened with the strands of a rope, meaning: magic that has been made firm. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Until his bitter firmness was established upon a secret, sincere in resolve, neither softened nor weakened."*

Anas, Yaman, Mujahid, al-Kisa'i, and al-Farra' said, and al-Nahhas chose this: mustamirr means passing and departing, quickly ceasing. They reasoned by this to console themselves. It was also said: mustamirr means extremely bitter, that is, something that we find loathsome and bitter. It is said: "the thing became bitter" (marra al-shay'u wa amarra) when it became bitter, and "he made it bitter" (amarra ghayrahu wa marrahu) when he made something else bitter, and it is both intransitive and transitive. It was also said: mustamirr means that one part resembles another, that is, its actions continued in this manner of imaginings. It was also said: mustamirr means passing from the earth to the sky, that is, his magic reached the point that he bewitched the moon.

﴿And they denied﴾: that is, the signs and the one who brought them. That is, they said, "This is continuous magic; Muhammad has bewitched us."

﴿And followed their desires﴾: that is, the lusts of their souls and what they craved.

﴿Wa kullu amrin mustaqirr﴾: read with a kasra on the qaf and a damma on the ra'. It may be the subject (mubtada') or the predicate (khabar). Muqatil said: it has an end to which it arrives. Al-Kalbi said: it has a reality (haqiqa) that it settles into. Whatever is in this world will become manifest, and whatever is in the Hereafter will be known. Qatadah said: its meaning is that good settles upon the people of good and evil upon the people of evil. It has also been said: the truth settles, manifest and firm, and falsehood is destroyed and gone. It has also been said: every matter of theirs and of His settles into humiliation or victory in this world, and into happiness or misery in the Hereafter.

Shaybah recited mustaqarr with a fatha on the qaf, and it is reported from Nafi'. Abu Hatim said: there is no basis for a fatha on the qaf. End of quotation. It has been explained as the omission of a modifier, meaning "possessing settledness" or "a time of settledness."

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Ali recited mustaqirrin with a kasra on both the qaf and the ra', as an attribute (sifah) of amr.

Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning that wa kullu is conjoined (ma'tuf) to al-sa'ah, so that the sense is: "The Hour has drawn near, and every settled matter has drawn near, settling and its state becoming clear." This is far-fetched, because of the long separation by three clauses, and it is far-fetched that such a construction would occur in Arabic speech, as in the example: "I ate bread, and I struck Zayd, and if Zayd comes, I honor him, and he traveled to the people of so-and-so, and meat," so that "and meat" would be conjoined to "bread." Indeed, nothing like it is found in the speech of the Arabs.

The author of al-Lawami' explained it as the predicate of kull, so it is nominative (marfu') in origin, but it is put in the genitive (majrur) by proximity (lil-mujawarah). This is not sound, because genitive by proximity is an extreme anomaly (ghayat al-shudhudh), and because it is not attested in the predicate of a subject; it is attested only in the attribute, though grammarians disagree about its occurrence. The easier view is that the predicate is omitted, its meaning being indicated by context, and the estimate is: ﴿wa kullu amrin mustaqirrun﴾ bali'uhu, "will reach them," because before it is ﴿and they denied and followed their desires﴾. That is: "And every matter is settled for them by decree, good or evil, and they will reach it." It has also been said: the predicate is "a far-reaching wisdom" (hikmah baligha), meaning: "And every matter that is settled is a far-reaching wisdom." In that case ﴿And there has already come to them of the reports that which contains a deterrent﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) between the subject and its predicate.

﴿Wa laqad ja'ahum mina al-anba'﴾: that is, of the reports contained in the Qur'an concerning the destruction of those who denied the prophets, and what they will come to in the Hereafter.

﴿ma fihi muzdajar﴾: that is, a restraining deterrence (izdijar radi') for them from what they are in, or a place of deterrence and restraint; that is, that is a place of deterrence, or a likely cause of it.

It has been read as muzzajar, by replacing the t of the infi'al form with z and assimilating the z into it. Zayd ibn Ali recited muzjir, an active participle of azjara, meaning "one who has a deterrent," like a'shaba, "one who has grass." The majority read ﴿hikmatun baligha﴾ with both in the nominative. They permitted that hikmah be a substitute (badal) for muzdajar or for ma, or the predicate of an omitted subject. The opinion of one who made it the predicate of kull in the reading of one who recited "mustaqirr" in the genitive has already been mentioned. Al-Yamani recited hikmatan baligatan with both in the accusative, as a circumstantial (hal) of ma, whether ma is a relative pronoun or an indefinite noun specified by its attribute. Hikmah is described as baligha because it reaches (tablughu) other things.

﴿Fa ma tughni al-nudhur﴾: with these disbelievers.

Then He consoled His Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them, for warning is of no benefit among them.

Then He mentioned some of the states of the Hereafter and what they will come to, since that is connected to the drawing near of the Hour, saying: ﴿On the day when the caller calls﴾. The word yawm is governed by an implied verb, "remember," as said by al-Rummani, or by "they will come forth." Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "turn away from them until a day," but this is weak both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. As for wording, it omits ila ("until"). As for meaning, his turning away from them is not specifically tied to ﴿the day when the caller calls﴾.

They permitted that it be governed by His saying ﴿Fa ma tughni al-nudhur﴾, with ﴿So turn away from them﴾ being a parenthetical clause. It may also be governed by His saying ﴿The disbelievers will say﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]; governed by an implied "wait"; governed by His saying ﴿So turn away﴾, though this is very weak; or governed by mustaqirr, which is also far-fetched.

The waw in yad'u was omitted from the orthography (rasm) following the pronunciation, and the ya' in al-da'i was dropped for lightness, treating the definite article al- as a substitute for what replaces it, which is tanwin. (p-172) Al-jadath: the grave. Its th (ث) may be changed to f (ف), so it is said jadaf, just as they changed thumma (ثُمَّ) to fumma (فُمَّ). The water poured forth (infahara al-ma'): it descended with force and abundance. The poet said:

*"The east wind turned it, then there passed over it a heavy downpour from the south, pouring forth."*

Al-dusur: the nails with which the ship is fastened. Its singular is dissar, like kitab and kutub. It is said: "I fastened the ship" (dasartu al-safina) when I secured it with nails. Al-Layth and the author of al-Sihah said: al-dusur are cords with which the planks of the ship are tied. Al-sarsar: that which is severe in sound or in cold. It is either from the screech (sarir) of a door, which is its sound, or from al-sirr, which is cold. It is an原 root built on the pattern fa'lal according to the majority of scholars. Al-'ajuz: the back part of a thing. Al-munqa'ir: that which is uprooted from its base. "I uprooted the tree" (qa'artu al-shajarata qa'ran) means I pulled it from its root, and it became uprooted (infaqara). For a well: "I descended until I reached its bottom." For a vessel: "I drank what was in it until I reached its bottom." "I made its well deep" (aqra'tuhu al-bi'r) means I made a bottom for it. Al-ashir: the insolent. It has been read ashira with a kasra, yash'aru ashaaran, so he is ashir, ashir, and ashran, and the people are ushara, like sakran and sukara. Saqar: a proper name for Hell, derived from saqarat-hu al-nar (the fire scorched him) with a sin, or from saqartu-hu with a sad when you blackened him. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"When the sun melts, he shields himself from its scorching heat with the branches of a tree of mixed shade, in a sandhill grown dense."*

Saqar is not declined (did not take tanwin) because it is a proper noun and feminine. The vowel of its middle letter is treated as if it were the fourth letter, as in Zaynab.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ ﴿They denied and followed their desires, and every matter will be settled.﴾ ﴿There had certainly come to them of the news that which contained a deterrent.﴾ ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings did not avail.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them. The day the caller calls to a terrible thing,﴾ ﴿with eyes humbled, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:7) ﴿Hastening toward the caller, the disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:8) ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and they denied Our servant and said, "He is a madman," and he was rebuked.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:9) ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overpowered, so help me."﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:10) ﴿So We opened the gates of the heaven with water pouring forth.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:11) ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:12) ﴿And We carried him on a vessel of planks and nails,﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:13) ﴿sailing under Our eyes, as a reward for one who had been denied.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:14) ﴿And We left it as a sign. Is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:15) ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:16) ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance. Is there anyone who will remember?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:17)

.

(p-172) Al-jadath: the grave. Its th (ث) may be changed to f (ف), so it is said jadaf, just as they changed thumma (ثُمَّ) to fumma (فُمَّ). The water poured forth (infahara al-ma'): it descended with force and abundance. The poet said:

*"The east wind turned it, then there passed over it a heavy downpour from the south, pouring forth."*

Al-dusur: the nails with which the ship is fastened. Its singular is dissar, like kitab and kutub. It is said: "I fastened the ship" (dasartu al-safina) when I secured it with nails. Al-Layth and the author of al-Sihah said: al-dusur are cords with which the planks of the ship are tied. Al-sarsar: that which is severe in sound or in cold. It is either from the screech (sarir) of a door, which is its sound, or from al-sirr, which is cold. It is an原 root built on the pattern fa'lal according to the majority of scholars. Al-'ajuz: the back part of a thing. Al-munqa'ir: that which is uprooted from its base. "I uprooted the tree" (qa'artu al-shajarata qa'ran) means I pulled it from its root, and it became uprooted (infaqara). For a well: "I descended until I reached its bottom." For a vessel: "I drank what was in it until I reached its bottom." "I made its well deep" (aqra'tuhu al-bi'r) means I made a bottom for it. Al-ashir: the insolent. It has been read ashira with a kasra, yash'aru ashaaran, so he is ashir, ashir, and ashran, and the people are ushara, like sakran and sukara. Saqar: a proper name for Hell, derived from saqarat-hu al-nar (the fire scorched him) with a sin, or from saqartu-hu with a sad when you blackened him. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"When the sun melts, he shields himself from its scorching heat with the branches of a tree of mixed shade, in a sandhill grown dense."*

Saqar is not declined (did not take tanwin) because it is a proper noun and feminine. The vowel of its middle letter is treated as if it were the fourth letter, as in Zaynab.

﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split.﴾ ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ ﴿They denied and followed their desires, and every matter will be settled.﴾ ﴿There had certainly come to them of the news that which contained a deterrent.﴾ ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings did not avail.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them. The day the caller calls to a terrible thing,﴾ ﴿with eyes humbled, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:7) ﴿Hastening toward the caller, the disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day."﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:8) ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and they denied Our servant and said, "He is a madman," and he was rebuked.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:9) ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overpowered, so help me."﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:10) ﴿So We opened the gates of the heaven with water pouring forth.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:11) ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:12) ﴿And We carried him on a vessel of planks and nails,﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:13) ﴿sailing under Our eyes, as a reward for one who had been denied.﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:14) ﴿And We left it as a sign. Is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:15) ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:16) ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance. Is there anyone who will remember?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:17) .

(p-173) This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars (al-jumhur). It was also said that it was revealed on the Day of Badr. Muqatil said: it is Meccan except for three verses. The first is ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united force, victorious"?﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:44), and the last is ﴿more calamitous and bitter﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:46).

The occasion of its revelation was that the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Messenger (ﷺ), "If you are truthful, split the moon for us into two halves," and they promised him belief if he did so. This was the night of Badr. He asked his Lord, and the moon split, one half upon al-Safa and one half upon Qay'qa'an. The people of Makkah said, "This is a heavenly sign that magic cannot affect." Abu Jahl said, "Wait until the people of the deserts come to us. If they report its splitting, then it is true; otherwise, Muhammad has bewitched our eyes." They came and reported the splitting of the moon, so Abu Jahl turned away and said, ﴿Continuous magic﴾ (Al-Qamar 54:2).

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the moon was split into two pieces, one piece over al-Suwayda' and one piece over al-Hudaybiyah. And from him: the moon split twice in Makkah. And from him: it split into two halves, one half that departed and one half that remained.

The connection of the beginning of the surah to the end of what precedes it is evident. He said, ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾ (al-Najm 53:57), and He said, ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾. Among those who witnessed the splitting of the moon were Ibn Mas'ud and Jubayr ibn Mut'im. Ibn 'Umar, Anas, Hudhayfah, and Ibn 'Abbas reported it. "When Allah showed the people the splitting of the moon, the Messenger (ﷺ) said, 'Bear witness.'" The polytheists said at that time, "Muhammad has bewitched us," and some of them said, "He has bewitched the moon."

The Ummah is in agreement against the view of the one who claimed that His saying ﴿and the moon has split﴾ means that it will split on the Day of Resurrection. What refutes this from the verse is His saying ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic."﴾ Therefore, this statement would not fit unless it came after the manifestation of what they had specifically asked for, namely the splitting of the moon.

It was also said: they asked for a sign in general, so He showed them this heavenly sign, which is among the greatest signs, and this is an effect in the upper world. Hudhayfah recited: "and the moon has split" (wa qad inshaqqa al-qamar), meaning "has drawn near." The splitting of the moon is among the signs of its drawing near, just as you say, "The emir has come, and the one bringing good news of his arrival has come." Hudhayfah delivered a sermon in al-Mada'in and then said, "Indeed the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split in the time of your Prophet."

There is no consideration given to the statement of al-Hasan that the meaning is: when the Hour comes, the moon will split after the second blast. Nor is there consideration given to the view of one who said that its splitting is an expression for the splitting of darkness when it rises through it, so the meaning is: the matter became manifest. The Arabs use the moon as an example of what is clear, just as dawn is called falaq at the splitting of darkness from it, and splitting may be expressed by the word for cleaving. Al-Nabighah said:

*"When they turned their backs, and there was a clamor among them, a caller called to us at the splitting of the dawn."*

These are corrupt statements, and were it not that the commentators mentioned them, I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely.

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾. It has been read as yurawa (passive), meaning: it is their nature and state that whenever they see what indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) of the dazzling signs, they turn away from believing in him and in that sign. The sentence came in conditional form to show that in the future they will be in a state like their state in the past, and they will say: ﴿Continuous magic﴾, meaning: lasting. From this is the saying of the poet:

(p-174) *"Indeed, the world is only nights and days, and nothing upright remains lasting."*

That is, nothing lasting. When they saw the signs following one another without interruption, they said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Akhfash said: mustamirr means tightly bound, firmly fastened with the strands of a rope, meaning: magic that has been made firm. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Until his bitter firmness was established upon a secret, sincere in resolve, neither softened nor weakened."*

Anas, Yaman, Mujahid, al-Kisa'i, and al-Farra' said, and al-Nahhas chose this: mustamirr means passing and departing, quickly ceasing. They reasoned by this to console themselves. It was also said: mustamirr means extremely bitter, that is, something that we find loathsome and bitter. It is said: "the thing became bitter" (marra al-shay'u wa amarra) when it became bitter, and "he made it bitter" (amarra ghayrahu wa marrahu) when he made something else bitter, and it is both intransitive and transitive. It was also said: mustamirr means that one part resembles another, that is, its actions continued in this manner of imaginings. It was also said: mustamirr means passing from the earth to the sky, that is, his magic reached the point that he bewitched the moon.

﴿And they denied﴾: that is, the signs and the one who brought them. That is, they said, "This is continuous magic; Muhammad has bewitched us."

﴿And followed their desires﴾: that is, the lusts of their souls and what they craved.

﴿Wa kullu amrin mustaqirr﴾: read with a kasra on the qaf and a damma on the ra'. It may be the subject (mubtada') or the predicate (khabar). Muqatil said: it has an end to which it arrives. Al-Kalbi said: it has a reality (haqiqa) that it settles into. Whatever is in this world will become manifest, and whatever is in the Hereafter will be known. Qatadah said: its meaning is that good settles upon the people of good and evil upon the people of evil. It has also been said: the truth settles, manifest and firm, and falsehood is destroyed and gone. It has also been said: every matter of theirs and of His settles into humiliation or victory in this world, and into happiness or misery in the Hereafter.

Shaybah recited mustaqarr with a fatha on the qaf, and it is reported from Nafi'. Abu Hatim said: there is no basis for a fatha on the qaf. End of quotation. It has been explained as the omission of a modifier, meaning "possessing settledness" or "a time of settledness."

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Ali recited mustaqirrin with a kasra on both the qaf and the ra', as an attribute (sifah) of amr.

Al-Zamakhshari explained it as meaning that wa kullu is conjoined (ma'tuf) to al-sa'ah, so that the sense is: "The Hour has drawn near, and every settled matter has drawn near, settling and its state becoming clear." This is far-fetched, because of the long separation by three clauses, and it is far-fetched that such a construction would occur in Arabic speech, as in the example: "I ate bread, and I struck Zayd, and if Zayd comes, I honor him, and he traveled to the people of so-and-so, and meat," so that "and meat" would be conjoined to "bread." Indeed, nothing like it is found in the speech of the Arabs.

The author of al-Lawami' explained it as the predicate of kull, so it is nominative (marfu') in origin, but it is put in the genitive (majrur) by proximity (lil-mujawarah). This is not sound, because genitive by proximity is an extreme anomaly (ghayat al-shudhudh), and because it is not attested in the predicate of a subject; it is attested only in the attribute, though grammarians disagree about its occurrence. The easier view is that the predicate is omitted, its meaning being indicated by context, and the estimate is: ﴿wa kullu amrin mustaqirrun﴾ bali'uhu, "will reach them," because before it is ﴿and they denied and followed their desires﴾. That is: "And every matter is settled for them by decree, good or evil, and they will reach it." It has also been said: the predicate is "a far-reaching wisdom" (hikmah baligha), meaning: "And every matter that is settled is a far-reaching wisdom." In that case ﴿And there has already come to them of the reports that which contains a deterrent﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) between the subject and its predicate.

﴿Wa laqad ja'ahum mina al-anba'﴾: that is, of the reports contained in the Qur'an concerning the destruction of those who denied the prophets, and what they will come to in the Hereafter.

﴿ma fihi muzdajar﴾: that is, a restraining deterrence (izdijar radi') for them from what they are in, or a place of deterrence and restraint; that is, that is a place of deterrence, or a likely cause of it.

It has been read as muzzajar, by replacing the t of the infi'al form with z and assimilating the z into it. Zayd ibn Ali recited muzjir, an active participle of azjara, meaning "one who has a deterrent," like a'shaba, "one who has grass." The majority read ﴿hikmatun baligha﴾ with both in the nominative. They permitted that hikmah be a substitute (badal) for muzdajar or for ma, or the predicate of an omitted subject. The opinion of one who made it the predicate of kull in the reading of one who recited "mustaqirr" in the genitive has already been mentioned. Al-Yamani recited hikmatan baligatan with both in the accusative, as a circumstantial (hal) of ma, whether ma is a relative pronoun or an indefinite noun specified by its attribute. Hikmah is described as baligha because it reaches (tablughu) other things.

﴿Fa ma tughni al-nudhur﴾: with these disbelievers.

Then He consoled His Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them, for warning is of no benefit among them.

Then He mentioned some of the states of the Hereafter and what they will come to, since that is connected to the drawing near of the Hour, saying: ﴿On the day when the caller calls﴾. The word yawm is governed by an implied verb, "remember," as said by al-Rummani, or by "they will come forth." Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "turn away from them until a day," but this is weak both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. As for wording, it omits ila ("until"). As for meaning, his turning away from them is not specifically tied to ﴿the day when the caller calls﴾.

They permitted that it be governed by His saying ﴿Fa ma tughni al-nudhur﴾, with ﴿So turn away from them﴾ being a parenthetical clause. It may also be governed by His saying ﴿The disbelievers will say﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]; governed by an implied "wait"; governed by His saying ﴿So turn away﴾, though this is very weak; or governed by mustaqirr, which is also far-fetched.

The waw in yad'u was omitted from the orthography (rasm) following the pronunciation, and the ya' in al-da'i was dropped for lightness, treating the definite article al- as a substitute for what replaces it, which is tanwin. Just as it is dropped with tanwin, it is dropped with al-. The caller (al-da'i) is Israfil, or Jibril, or another angel appointed for that task; there are several opinions.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 54, verses 7–17 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Jumhur read ﴿نُكُرٍ﴾ [al-Qamar: 6] with a *ḍamma* on the *kaf* (*nukur*). It is an adjective on the pattern *fu'ul*, which is rare among adjectives. From it comes *rajulun shulul*, meaning a man who is light in need; *naqatun ujud*, a she-camel that is swift; *mishyatun sujuh*, an easy gait; and *rawḍatun unuf*, a meadow that has not been grazed.

Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Kathir and Shibl read it with a *sukun* on the *kaf*, as in the forms *shughul* and *shughl*, and *'usr* and *'usur*.

Mujahid, Abu Qilaba, al-Jahdari and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *nukkira*, a past verb in the passive voice, meaning that it was not recognised and so was made unfamiliar.

Al-Khalil said: *al-nukur* is a description of a severe matter, and *al-wajal* is a calamity. That is, the souls reject it because they have never known anything like it, and it is the Day of Resurrection. Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri said:

*Advance, Maḥāj, for it is a day of nukur,*
*my like against your like, defending and returning.*

Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj and al-Jumhur read *khushshaʿan*, which is a broken plural (*jam' taksir*). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read *khashiʿan* in the singular. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *khashiʿa*, feminine. The broken plural is more common in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda said: all of it is permissible. The quotation ends here. An example of the broken plural is the poet's words:

*With a straight, flexible spear whose joints are sound,*
*and with a bright, keen sword that cuts through helmets.*

An example of the singular is his words:

*And men whose faces are handsome,*
*from the Ayad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'add.*

Another poet said:

*The riders hurl through the wide roads, the reins loose on their necks,*
*the bridles of their young camels hanging loose.*

*Khushshaʿan*, *khashiʿan* and *khashiʿa* are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in *yakhrujūna* (they come out), and the governing word is *yakhrujūna*, because it is a verb that can be inflected (*mutaṣarrif*). This shows the invalidity of the view of al-Jarmi, because it is not permitted for a circumstantial clause to precede its verb, even if the verb is inflected. The Arabs have said *shattā ta'ubbu al-ḥalbah* (scattered, the milking-troop returns), where *shattā* is a circumstantial clause and it precedes its governing word *ta'ubbu*, because that is an inflected verb. The poet said:

*Hard things become easy quickly for those of wisdom,*
*when they meet them with a sincere hope.*

So *sarī'an* is a circumstantial clause and it precedes its governing word *yahūnu*.

It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive (*majrūr*) in *'anhum* in His words ﴿فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. It has also been said that it is an object of *yad'u* (he calls), meaning a people who are humbled, or a group who are humbled, but this is far-fetched.

As for whoever reads *khāshiʿan* in the singular with masculine agreement, it is according to the estimate *takhsha' abṣāruhum* (their eyes are humbled). Whoever reads *khāshiʿa* with feminine agreement, it is according to the estimate *takhsha'* (it is humbled). Whoever reads *khushshaʿan* as a broken plural, it is because the plural agrees with what follows it, which is *abṣāruhum*, and agrees with the pronoun that is the subject of the circumstance in *yakhrujūna*. This is like the expression *marartu bi-rijālin kirāmin ābā'uhum* (I passed by noble men whose fathers ...).

Al-Zamakhshari said: *khushshaʿan* is according to *yakhshaʿna abṣāruhum* (their eyes humble themselves), and this is the dialect of those who say *akalūnī al-barāghīth* (the fleas ate me), and they are the Tayy. The quotation ends here. But the broken plural is not treated like the sound plural, so that it would be in that rare and scant dialect.

Sibawayh has stated explicitly that the broken plural is more common in the speech of the Arabs, so how can it be more common when it is in that rare and scant dialect? Likewise al-Farra' said, when he mentioned the singular, masculine and feminine, and the broken plural: because the adjective, whenever it precedes a group, it is permissible for it to take all of these forms, and the plural agrees with its wording, so it is more fitting. The quotation ends here. That dialect is only applied when the plural is formed with the *waw* and *nun* suffix, as in *marartu bi-qawmin karīmīna ābā'uhum* (I passed by noble people whose fathers ...). Al-Zamakhshari analogised the broken plural with this sound masculine plural, and this is a faulty analogy. It is refuted by the transmission from the Arabs that the broken plural is better than the singular, as we have mentioned from Sibawayh, and as the words of al-Farra' also indicate.

He also permitted that there be a pronoun in *khushshaʿan*, with *abṣāruhum* as an appositive (*badal*) to it. It has been read: *khushshaʿun abṣāruhum*, where it is a clause in the place of a circumstantial clause, and *khushshaʿun* is a predicate placed before its subject. The humbling of the eyes is a metaphor for abasement, and it is more evident in the eyes than in the rest of the limbs. Likewise the actions of the soul, of humiliation, honour, shame, arrogance, fear and other things.

﴿كَأنَّهم جَرادٌ مُنْتَشِرٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 7]: *ka'annahum jarādun muntashir* (as if they were scattered locusts) is also a circumstantial clause. It compares them to locusts in their number and their surging. It is said: they came like locusts in a great army surging forward. It is also said: like flies. Their comparison with scattered moths has also come, and each of the locusts and the moths has a resemblance to those who come out on the Day of Gathering. It has been said: at first they will be like moths when they surge in fear, not knowing where to head, because the moth has no direction it aims for. Then they will be like scattered locusts when they turn towards the place of gathering and the caller. These are two comparisons with regard to two times. This is the view of Makki ibn Abi Talib.

﴿مُهْطِعِينَ﴾ [al-Qamar: 8] (*muhṭi'īna*, hastening): Abu 'Ubayda said: *musri'īna* (hurrying). From this is the poet's words:

*In Dijla is their home, and I have seen them,*
*in Dijla, hastening towards the sound.*

Another added: stretching out their necks. Another added: with trembling and dread, and a gaze fixed towards the goal, either out of fear or hope, or the like. Qatada said: *'āmidīn* (intending). Al-Dahhak said: *muqbilīn* (approaching). 'Ikrima said: opening their ears to the sound. Ibn 'Abbas said: looking. From this is the poet's words:

*Nimr ibn Sa'd has enslaved me, and I see him,*
*and Nimr ibn Sa'd is obedient to me and hastening.*

It has been said: lowering what is between their eyes. Sufyan said: their eyes are humbled towards the sky.

﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِرٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]: a hard day, because of what they witness of the signs of its terror, and what they expect of the evil of their outcome in it.

﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ﴾ [al-Qamar: 9]: that is, before the Quraysh, ﴿قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ (the people of Nuh) reject. In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a parable for them. The object of *kadhdhabat* is omitted, meaning the messengers rejected, so they rejected Nuh (peace be upon him). Because they were rejecting the messengers and denying prophethood altogether, they rejected Nuh, since he was among the messengers. It is also permissible that the omitted object be Nuh at the first of his coming to them, so they rejected him with a rejection that was followed by rejection, each time a generation of rejecters passed away, another generation of rejecters followed it.

In the phrase *'abdanā* (Our servant) there is an honour and a particularity of servanthood, like His saying ﴿وما أنْزَلْنا عَلى عَبْدِنا يَوْمَ الفُرْقانِ﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] and ﴿سُبْحانَ الَّذِي أسْرى بِعَبْدِهِ﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

﴿وقالُوا مَجْنُونٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 9]: that is, he is mad. When they saw the signs that indicated his truthfulness, they said: he is possessed by jinn. They were not content with rejecting him until they attributed madness to him, meaning he says what no sane person would accept, and this is an intensification of their rejection.

﴿وازْدُجِرَ فَدَعا رَبَّهُ أنِّي مَغْلُوبٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 9–10]: The apparent meaning is that His words *wa-zdujira* (and he was rebuked) are from the report of God the Exalted, meaning they berated and rebuked him with abuse and threats. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and he recited: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهِ يانُوحُ لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المَرْجُومِينَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 116] ("If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned"). It has been said: the meaning is that they did to him what requires him to be restrained from calling them, until he abandoned his call to them to faith and turned to calling down (evil) upon them. Mujahid said: *wa-zdujira* is part of their words, meaning they said, "and he is rebuked", that is, "he has been driven mad", meaning the jinn have rebuked him, taken away his mind, and deranged him.

Ibn Ishaq, 'Isa, al-A'mash and Zayd ibn 'Ali, and a report from 'Asim, read *inni* with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, either by the implied verb of speech according to the view of the Basrans, or by treating the prayer as if it were speech according to the view of the Kufans.

Al-Jumhur read it with a *fatḥa*, meaning *bi-anni maghlūb* (because I am overcome), that is, my people have overcome me, so they did not listen to me, and I despaired of their answering me.

﴿فانْتَصِرْ﴾ [al-Qamar: 10] (so take vengeance): that is, avenge yourself by a punishment that you send upon them. He only called down upon them after he despaired of them and their affair became grave. One of his people would choke him until he fell unconscious, and he had been saying: "O God, forgive my people, for they do not know." The object of *fa-ntasir* is omitted. It has been said: the estimate is *fa-ntasir lī minhum bi-an tuhlikahum* (so avenge me upon them by destroying them). It has also been said: *fa-ntasir li-nafsika* (so avenge yourself), since they rejected your messenger, and then the answer came. The Sufis have a view on ﴿مَغْلُوبٌ فانْتَصِرْ﴾ (overcome, so avenge), recounted by Ibn 'Atiyya, which is to be consulted in his book.

﴿فَفَتَحْنا﴾ [al-Qamar: 11] (So We opened): this explains that God the Exalted took vengeance upon them and punished them. It has been said: it is strange that they were asking for rain for years, and God the Exalted destroyed them with what they had sought.

﴿أبْوابَ السَّماءِ بِماءٍ﴾ [al-Qamar: 11] (the gates of heaven with water): He made the water as if it were an instrument by which something is opened, just as you say: "I opened the door with the key." It is as if the water came and opened the door, so he made the intended thing, which is the water, precede in existence the opening of the closed door. It is also permissible that the *bā'* (with) denote a circumstance, meaning it is connected with water pouring forth.

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Ya'qub read *fa-fattaḥnā* with a shadda (intensive form). Al-Jumhur read it without a shadda. *Abwāb al-samā'* (the gates of heaven): according to al-Jumhur this is a metaphor and a figure of speech, because the rain was so abundant that it was as if it were descending from gates, just as you say: "the mouths of the waterskins were opened", and "the drains of the sky flowed." 'Ali said, and al-Naqqash followed him: by the gates he means the Milky Way, which is the "scattering" of the sky like the scattering of a sack. Some people went to the view that it is literal: gates were opened in heaven from which the water flowed. Something similar is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the gates of heaven were opened without clouds, and they were not closed for forty days. Al-Suddi said: *munhamir* (pouring) means abundant. The poet said:

*My eyes, pour forth tears in abundance*
*for the best of the dwellers of Ma'add, both the desert-dweller and the settled.*

Al-Jumhur read ﴿وفَجَّرْنا﴾ (and We caused to gush forth) with a shadda on the *jīm*. 'Abdullah and his companions, Abu Ḥaywa and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read it without a shadda. It is well-known that *'ayn* is a term with several meanings. The apparent meaning is that it is literal for the seeing eye and figurative for other things. In the case of something other than water, it is a well-known and predominant figure of speech.

*'Uyūnan* (springs) is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*), as if the whole earth had become springs gushing forth. This is more eloquent than "and We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth." Whoever forbids the occurrence of a specification from the object, treats it as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and it is a circumstantial clause in prospect (*ḥāl muqaddara*). Some have treated it as a second object, as if *wa-fajjarnā* were taken to mean "We made, by causing to gush forth, *al-arḍa 'uyūnan* (the earth into springs)." It has been said: the earth gushed forth for forty days.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿فالتَقى الماءُ﴾ (so the waters met), where *al-mā'* is a collective noun, and the meaning is the water of the sky and the water of the earth. 'Ali, al-Ḥasan, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Jahdari read *al-mā'ān* (the two waters). Al-Ḥasan also read *al-māwān* (the two waters), by changing the *hamza* to a *waw*, like the form *'ilbāwān*. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Ḥasan read *māwān*, by converting the *hamza* into a *waw*, as in their saying *'ilbāwān*. The quotation ends here. He compared the *hamza* which is a substitute for a *hā'* in *al-mā'* with the *hamza* of extension in *'ilbā'* (a kind of plant). It is also narrated from al-Ḥasan: *al-māyān*, by converting the *hamza* into a *yā'*. In both readings there is an irregularity.

﴿عَلى أمْرٍ قَدْ قُدِرَ﴾ [al-Qamar: 12] (upon a matter that had been decreed): that is, upon a state and a rank that had been determined in eternity. It has been said: upon measures that had been arranged at the time of their meeting. It is related that the water of the earth was seventeen cubits, and the rain from the sky descended to complete forty cubits. It has been said: the water of the earth was greater. It has been said: they were equal, so that from the sky there descended the same amount as came out of the earth.

It has been said: ﴿عَلى أمْرٍ قَدْ قُدِرَ﴾ means that in the Preserved Tablet it was written that it would happen, and it is the destruction of the people of Nuh (peace be upon him) by the Flood. This is the preferred view, because every story that is mentioned after this story mentions the destruction of those who rejected the messengers in it, so this is an allusion to the destruction of the people of Nuh. For this reason He mentions the deliverance of Nuh after it in His words: ﴿وحَمَلْناهُ عَلى ذاتِ ألْواحٍ ودُسُرٍ﴾ [al-Qamar: 13] ("And We bore him upon one of planks and nails").

Abu Ḥaywa read *qudirra* with a shadda on the *dāl*. The majority read it with a light *dāl*. *Dhāt al-alwāḥ wa-al-dusur* (the one of planks and nails) is the ship which Nuh (peace be upon him) built. These two descriptions imply that it is the ship. So this is an adjective that stands in the place of the thing described and takes its place, similar to *qamīṣī masrūdatun min ḥadīd* (my shirt is a coat of mail of iron), meaning a coat of mail. This is from the eloquent and the wondrous in speech. If you combined the adjective with the thing described in it, it would not be eloquent. *Al-dusur* means the nails, as the majority said. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn 'Abbas said: the forepart of the ship, because it pushes (*tadsuru*) the water, that is, it drives it away, and *al-dasr* is driving away. Mujahid and others said: the belly of the ship. And from him also: the ribs of the ship. And from him also: the sides of the ship. It runs on that meeting water with protection and safekeeping from Us, so that whoever was in it was saved, and others were drowned.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "bi-a'yunina" means "with Our revelation." It was also said: "with Our command." And it was said: "with Our protectors." It is said: "So-and-so is one of the eyes of God Most High," meaning: one of His protectors (awliya'). It was also said: "with the springs of water which We caused to gush forth." And it was said: those among the angels who guarded it, He named "eyes."

Zayd ibn Ali and Abu al-Sammal read "bi-a'yunna" with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters); the majority read it with fakk (without assimilation).

"Jaza'an" means: as a recompense (mujazah). "Li-man kana kufira" means: for Noah, peace be upon him, since he was a blessing that God bestowed upon his people so that they would believe, but they rejected it. The meaning is that His carrying him in the ark, and those who believed with him, was a recompense for him for his patience with his people over nine hundred years. "Man" is a reference to Noah. It was said: "bi-man kufira" means: for the one whose prophethood was denied. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "man" refers to God Most High, as if it said: out of anger and for the sake of God Most High, meaning He avenged Himself, so He drowned the disbelievers and saved the believers. These two interpretations of "man" are according to the reading of the majority.

"Kufira" is in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul). Maslamah ibn Muharib read it with a sukun on the fa', lightening the form fu'il, as the poet said:

"Had musk and ben-oil been pressed from it, it would have been pressed."

He intends: "law 'usira" (if it had been pressed).

Zayd ibn Ruman, Qatadah and 'Isa read "kafara" in the active voice, so "man" refers to the people of Noah: that is, what arose from the opening of the gates of heaven with water, the gushing of the springs of the earth, and the meeting of the two waters, from the drowning of the people of Noah, peace and blessings be upon him, was a recompense for them for their disbelief. "Kufira" is the predicate of "kana." In this there is evidence for the occurrence of a past-tense verb as the predicate of "kana" without "qad"; this is the position of the Basrans and others. He says: "qad" must be present, either explicitly or implicitly, although it is permissible if "kana" here is extra (za'idah), i.e., "li-man kufira." The pronoun in "tarakna-ha" refers to the deed and the account.

Qatadah, al-Naqqash and others said: it refers to the ship, and that God Most High preserved its timber until some of the early people of this community saw it. Qatadah said: "How many a ship after it has become ashes!"

The majority read "muddakir" with idgham of the dhal into the dal, which replaced the ta' of the ifti'al form. Qatadah, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah, read it with the dhal, having assimilated the second letter into the first. The author of Kitab al-Lawami' and Qatadah said: "fa-hal min mudhakkir" is an active participle from tadhkir, meaning one who reminds himself or others of the past stories. End of quotation. It was also read "muddatakir" in its original form.

"Fa-kayfa kana 'adhabi wa-nudhur": this is an expression of awe at the punishment that befell the people of Noah and an exaltation of it, for He utterly uprooted them all and cut off their last trace, so that none of them escaped. That is: how was the outcome of My warning? "Nudhur" is the plural of "nadhir," meaning warning. This contains a reproach to Quraysh about what befell the like of those who denied. If "kana" is a defective verb (naqisah), then "kayfa" is in the place of the predicate of "kana"; if it is a complete verb (tammah), then "kayfa" is in the accusative place as a circumstantial. The interrogation here is not meant in its literal sense; rather the meaning is to remind them of what befell them.

"Wa-laqad yassarna": that is, We made easy, "al-Qur'an li-l-dhikr": that is, for remembrance and admonition, because of what it contains of exhortation, promise and threat.

"Fa-hal min muddakir": Ibn Zayd said: "from one who takes heed." Qatadah said: "is there anyone seeking good?" Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "is there anyone who restrains himself from sins?" It was also said: "li-l-dhikr" means "for memorization," that is, We made it easy to memorize, because of the fine composition it contains, the soundness of its wording, its freedom from superfluity, the nobility and correctness of its meanings; therefore it has a connection to hearts.

"Fa-hal min muddakir": that is, is there anyone seeking to memorize it so that he may be assisted in it, and so that its admonitions and sciences remain present in the soul. Ibn Jubayr said: no part of the divine books has been committed to memory except the Qur'an. It was also said: "yassarna" means "prepared," that is, We prepared "al-Qur'an li-l-dhikr," just as they say: "he made his she-camel ready for the journey" when he saddled it, and "he made his horse ready for the raid" when he saddled it and bridled it. The poet said:

"I stood up to it with the bridle, made ready; there, what I used to do repays me."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 54, verses 7–17 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Jumhur read ﴿نُكُرٍ﴾ [al-Qamar: 6] with a *ḍamma* on the *kaf* (*nukur*). It is an adjective on the pattern *fu'ul*, which is rare among adjectives. From it comes *rajulun shulul*, meaning a man who is light in need; *naqatun ujud*, a she-camel that is swift; *mishyatun sujuh*, an easy gait; and *rawḍatun unuf*, a meadow that has not been grazed.

Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Kathir and Shibl read it with a *sukun* on the *kaf*, as in the forms *shughul* and *shughl*, and *'usr* and *'usur*.

Mujahid, Abu Qilaba, al-Jahdari and Zayd ibn 'Ali read *nukkira*, a past verb in the passive voice, meaning that it was not recognised and so was made unfamiliar.

Al-Khalil said: *al-nukur* is a description of a severe matter, and *al-wajal* is a calamity. That is, the souls reject it because they have never known anything like it, and it is the Day of Resurrection. Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri said:

*Advance, Maḥāj, for it is a day of nukur,*
*my like against your like, defending and returning.*

Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj and al-Jumhur read *khushshaʿan*, which is a broken plural (*jam' taksir*). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read *khashiʿan* in the singular. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *khashiʿa*, feminine. The broken plural is more common in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda said: all of it is permissible. The quotation ends here. An example of the broken plural is the poet's words:

*With a straight, flexible spear whose joints are sound,*
*and with a bright, keen sword that cuts through helmets.*

An example of the singular is his words:

*And men whose faces are handsome,*
*from the Ayad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'add.*

Another poet said:

*The riders hurl through the wide roads, the reins loose on their necks,*
*the bridles of their young camels hanging loose.*

*Khushshaʿan*, *khashiʿan* and *khashiʿa* are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in *yakhrujūna* (they come out), and the governing word is *yakhrujūna*, because it is a verb that can be inflected (*mutaṣarrif*). This shows the invalidity of the view of al-Jarmi, because it is not permitted for a circumstantial clause to precede its verb, even if the verb is inflected. The Arabs have said *shattā ta'ubbu al-ḥalbah* (scattered, the milking-troop returns), where *shattā* is a circumstantial clause and it precedes its governing word *ta'ubbu*, because that is an inflected verb. The poet said:

*Hard things become easy quickly for those of wisdom,*
*when they meet them with a sincere hope.*

So *sarī'an* is a circumstantial clause and it precedes its governing word *yahūnu*.

It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive (*majrūr*) in *'anhum* in His words ﴿فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. It has also been said that it is an object of *yad'u* (he calls), meaning a people who are humbled, or a group who are humbled, but this is far-fetched.

As for whoever reads *khāshiʿan* in the singular with masculine agreement, it is according to the estimate *takhsha' abṣāruhum* (their eyes are humbled). Whoever reads *khāshiʿa* with feminine agreement, it is according to the estimate *takhsha'* (it is humbled). Whoever reads *khushshaʿan* as a broken plural, it is because the plural agrees with what follows it, which is *abṣāruhum*, and agrees with the pronoun that is the subject of the circumstance in *yakhrujūna*. This is like the expression *marartu bi-rijālin kirāmin ābā'uhum* (I passed by noble men whose fathers ...).

Al-Zamakhshari said: *khushshaʿan* is according to *yakhshaʿna abṣāruhum* (their eyes humble themselves), and this is the dialect of those who say *akalūnī al-barāghīth* (the fleas ate me), and they are the Tayy. The quotation ends here. But the broken plural is not treated like the sound plural, so that it would be in that rare and scant dialect.

Sibawayh has stated explicitly that the broken plural is more common in the speech of the Arabs, so how can it be more common when it is in that rare and scant dialect? Likewise al-Farra' said, when he mentioned the singular, masculine and feminine, and the broken plural: because the adjective, whenever it precedes a group, it is permissible for it to take all of these forms, and the plural agrees with its wording, so it is more fitting. The quotation ends here. That dialect is only applied when the plural is formed with the *waw* and *nun* suffix, as in *marartu bi-qawmin karīmīna ābā'uhum* (I passed by noble people whose fathers ...). Al-Zamakhshari analogised the broken plural with this sound masculine plural, and this is a faulty analogy. It is refuted by the transmission from the Arabs that the broken plural is better than the singular, as we have mentioned from Sibawayh, and as the words of al-Farra' also indicate.

He also permitted that there be a pronoun in *khushshaʿan*, with *abṣāruhum* as an appositive (*badal*) to it. It has been read: *khushshaʿun abṣāruhum*, where it is a clause in the place of a circumstantial clause, and *khushshaʿun* is a predicate placed before its subject. The humbling of the eyes is a metaphor for abasement, and it is more evident in the eyes than in the rest of the limbs. Likewise the actions of the soul, of humiliation, honour, shame, arrogance, fear and other things.

﴿كَأنَّهم جَرادٌ مُنْتَشِرٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 7]: *ka'annahum jarādun muntashir* (as if they were scattered locusts) is also a circumstantial clause. It compares them to locusts in their number and their surging. It is said: they came like locusts in a great army surging forward. It is also said: like flies. Their comparison with scattered moths has also come, and each of the locusts and the moths has a resemblance to those who come out on the Day of Gathering. It has been said: at first they will be like moths when they surge in fear, not knowing where to head, because the moth has no direction it aims for. Then they will be like scattered locusts when they turn towards the place of gathering and the caller. These are two comparisons with regard to two times. This is the view of Makki ibn Abi Talib.

﴿مُهْطِعِينَ﴾ [al-Qamar: 8] (*muhṭi'īna*, hastening): Abu 'Ubayda said: *musri'īna* (hurrying). From this is the poet's words:

*In Dijla is their home, and I have seen them,*
*in Dijla, hastening towards the sound.*

Another added: stretching out their necks. Another added: with trembling and dread, and a gaze fixed towards the goal, either out of fear or hope, or the like. Qatada said: *'āmidīn* (intending). Al-Dahhak said: *muqbilīn* (approaching). 'Ikrima said: opening their ears to the sound. Ibn 'Abbas said: looking. From this is the poet's words:

*Nimr ibn Sa'd has enslaved me, and I see him,*
*and Nimr ibn Sa'd is obedient to me and hastening.*

It has been said: lowering what is between their eyes. Sufyan said: their eyes are humbled towards the sky.

﴿يَوْمٌ عَسِرٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]: a hard day, because of what they witness of the signs of its terror, and what they expect of the evil of their outcome in it.

﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهُمْ﴾ [al-Qamar: 9]: that is, before the Quraysh, ﴿قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ (the people of Nuh) reject. In this there is a warning to the Quraysh and a parable for them. The object of *kadhdhabat* is omitted, meaning the messengers rejected, so they rejected Nuh (peace be upon him). Because they were rejecting the messengers and denying prophethood altogether, they rejected Nuh, since he was among the messengers. It is also permissible that the omitted object be Nuh at the first of his coming to them, so they rejected him with a rejection that was followed by rejection, each time a generation of rejecters passed away, another generation of rejecters followed it.

In the phrase *'abdanā* (Our servant) there is an honour and a particularity of servanthood, like His saying ﴿وما أنْزَلْنا عَلى عَبْدِنا يَوْمَ الفُرْقانِ﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] and ﴿سُبْحانَ الَّذِي أسْرى بِعَبْدِهِ﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

﴿وقالُوا مَجْنُونٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 9]: that is, he is mad. When they saw the signs that indicated his truthfulness, they said: he is possessed by jinn. They were not content with rejecting him until they attributed madness to him, meaning he says what no sane person would accept, and this is an intensification of their rejection.

﴿وازْدُجِرَ فَدَعا رَبَّهُ أنِّي مَغْلُوبٌ﴾ [al-Qamar: 9–10]: The apparent meaning is that His words *wa-zdujira* (and he was rebuked) are from the report of God the Exalted, meaning they berated and rebuked him with abuse and threats. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and he recited: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ تَنْتَهِ يانُوحُ لَتَكُونَنَّ مِنَ المَرْجُومِينَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 116] ("If you do not desist, O Nuh, you will surely be among the stoned"). It has been said: the meaning is that they did to him what requires him to be restrained from calling them, until he abandoned his call to them to faith and turned to calling down (evil) upon them.
