Thus do We reward those who give thanks.﴾ ﴿And he had warned them of Our assault, but they disputed the warnings.﴾ ﴿And they sought to seduce him from his guests, so We blinded their eyes: "Taste My punishment and warnings."﴾ ﴿And in the morning a settled punishment came upon them early.﴾ ﴿"So taste My punishment and warnings."﴾ ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance; so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿And the warnings certainly came to the family of Pharaoh.﴾ ﴿They denied all Our signs, so We seized them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Omnipotent.﴾ ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those? Or do you have immunity in the scriptures?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united company, victorious"?﴾ ﴿The company will be routed and they will turn their backs.﴾ ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and bitter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness.﴾ ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces: "Taste the touch of Saqar."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have created everything by measure.﴾ ﴿And Our command is but one word, like a glance of the eye.﴾ ﴿And We have destroyed your likes, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿And everything they did is in the scriptures.﴾ ﴿And every small and great matter is written down.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and rivers,﴾ ﴿in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent.﴾.

(p-182) The story of Lut, peace be upon him, and his people has already been related. The *ḥāṣib* (violent, pelting wind) derives from *al-ḥaṣbāʾ* (pebbles), and it is what is meant by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. ﴿Except the family of Lut﴾: it is said that this refers to his two daughters. ﴿At dawn (bi-saḥar)﴾: it means early morning, and for this reason it is given *tanwīn* (nunation, i.e., it takes the ending of an indefinite noun). ﴿A favor (niʿmatan)﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl min ajlihi*), meaning: We saved them because of Our bounty upon them; or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), because the meaning is: We bestowed a bounty by rescuing them. ﴿Thus do We reward﴾: that is, like that bounty and rescue, We reward ﴿those who give thanks﴾ for Our bounty, obey, and believe.

﴿And he had warned them of Our assault﴾: that is, Our seizing them with punishment. ﴿But they disputed﴾: that is, they doubted and engaged in that. ﴿The warnings﴾: that is, the admonition, or it may be the plural of *nadhīr* (warner).

﴿So We blinded﴾: Qatadah said: the blinding in reality was that Jibril, peace be upon him, drew his wing over their eyes, and their eyes became level with their faces. Abu ʿUbaydah said: their eyes were covered with a skin like a face. It was said: when Jibril struck them with his wing, he left them wandering, unable to find the door, until Lut, peace be upon him, brought them out. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said: this is a metaphor; He only veiled their perception, so they entered the house and saw nothing, and this was made like blinding. The majority read *fa-ṭamasnā* with a light *mīm*; Ibn Miqsam read it with a doubled *mīm*. ﴿Taste﴾: that is, I said to them through the tongues of the angels: "Taste."

﴿And in the morning He struck them early﴾: that is, at the beginning of the day and its earliest part, because of His words "shining" (*mushriqīn*) and "entering the morning" (*muṣbiḥīn*). The majority read *bukratan* with *tanwīn*, meaning *bukratan* from *al-bikr* (early), and so it takes the ending of an indefinite noun. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it without *tanwīn*.

﴿A settled punishment﴾: that is, no one removed it from them; rather, it continued with their death, then with what followed of the punishment of the grave, then the punishment of Hell.

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings﴾: this is emphasis and rebuke. The first was said at the blinding, and this at the morning arrival of the punishment. It was said: the purpose of repeating this and the repetition of ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy﴾ is to awaken the heart upon hearing each report from the reports of the former peoples, for admonition, and to renew alertness when they hear the urging toward that, lest heedlessness overtake them. The same is the rule for the repetition of ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 13] at each bounty enumerated in Surat al-Rahman, and the words ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 15] at each verse cited in Surat al-Mursalat. Likewise is the repetition of the stories in themselves, so that the lesson remains present in hearts and is mentioned at every time.

﴿And the warnings certainly came to the family of Pharaoh﴾: they are Musa, Harun, and other prophets, because the two of them presented to them what the messengers had warned of; or it may be the plural of *nadhīr* used as a verbal noun meaning warning. ﴿They denied Our signs﴾: these are the nine signs. The emphasis here is like that in His words: ﴿And We showed him all Our signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 56]. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿they denied﴾ and in ﴿so We seized them﴾ refers to the family of Pharaoh. It was also said that it refers to all the nations mentioned previously, and the speech is complete at the word ﴿the warnings﴾.

﴿So We seized them with the seizing of﴾ one who is ﴿Mighty﴾: unopposed; ﴿Omnipotent﴾: nothing can overcome Him.

﴿Are your disbelievers﴾: this is addressed to the people of Makkah. ﴿Better than those﴾: the reference is to the people of Nuh, Hud, Salih, and Lut, and to Pharaoh. The meaning is: are they better in strength, in the instruments of war, and in standing in this world, or less capable and more obstinate? Because they were not better, they are not exempt from punishment for disbelief in God. He placed them before a rebuke, meaning: your disbelievers are not better than those; rather, they are like them or worse than them, and you know what destruction befell those people, the complete uprooting, when they denied the messengers.

﴿Or do you have immunity in the scriptures﴾: that is, do you have in the divine books an immunity from the punishment of God, the Exalted? This was said by al-Dahhak, ʿIkrimah, and Ibn Zayd.

﴿Or do they say, "We are a united company﴾: that is, confident in our multitude, victorious by our strength, you say this out of self-admiration. The majority read *am yaqūlūna* with the third-person *yāʾ* (a shift to the third person), and likewise what follows, in the third person. Abu Haywah, Musa al-Aswari, and Abu al-Barahsam read it with the second-person *tāʾ* addressed to the disbelievers, following the address before it. They also read *sa-tahzimu al-jamʿa* with a *tāʾ* at the beginning, a *kasra* on the *zāy*, and a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*, addressed to the Messenger, ﷺ. Abu Haywah and Yaʿqub also read it with an open *nūn*, a *kasra* on the *zāy*, and a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*. The majority read it with a *yāʾ*, in the passive, with a *ḍamma* on the *ʿayn*. It was also reported from Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi ʿAbla: with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, in the active, and the *ʿayn* in the accusative, meaning: God will rout the company. The majority read *wa-yuwallūna* with the third-person *yāʾ*; Abu Haywah and Dawud ibn Abi Salim, from Abu ʿAmr, read it with the second-person *tāʾ*. Here *al-dubur* (the back) is a generic noun (*ism al-jins*). It occurs elsewhere as ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾ [al-Hashr: 12], which is the original form. The generic noun was made preferable here because it is the closing word of the verse (*fāṣila*). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and they will turn the back﴾, meaning *al-adbār* (the backs), as in the saying: "Eat in part of your belly so you will be chaste," and it was read as *al-adbār*. End of quote. But this is not like "your belly," because the singular *dubur* in this sense is not good, and the singular does not suit "your belly." In His words, the Exalted: ﴿The company will be routed﴾ is a promise from God to His Messenger, ﷺ, of the defeat of the company of Quraysh. The majority hold that the surah is Meccan, and the Messenger of God, ﷺ, recited it as evidence. It was also said that it was revealed on the day of Badr.

﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time﴾: he moved from those statements to the matter of the Hour, whose punishment is more severe for them than every defeat and battle.

﴿And the Hour is more calamitous﴾: that is, more terrible and more severe. *Al-dāhiya* is the bitterest calamity: the odious matter for which no way of repelling it is found; it is the great tragedy that befalls a person. ﴿Bitter (amarr)﴾ derives from *al-marāra* (bitterness); it is a metaphor for the difficulty of a thing upon the soul.

﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error﴾: that is, in confusion and turmoil in this world. ﴿And madness (suʿur)﴾: that is, burning in the Hereafter; they were placed in it because of their destination toward it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: and loss and madness; *al-suʿur* is madness, and something similar was mentioned in the story of Salih, peace be upon him.

﴿On the Day they are dragged﴾: they are pulled ﴿into the Fire﴾. In the reading of ʿAbdullah it is: ﴿into the Fire﴾ with *ilā*.

﴿Upon their faces, taste﴾: that is, it is said to them: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar.﴾ Mahbub, from Abu ʿAmr, read *massaqar* with the *sīn* assimilated into the *sīn*. Ibn Mujahid said: its assimilation is an error, because it is doubled. End of quote. But the presumption about Abu ʿAmr is that he did not assimilate until he deleted one of the two *sīns* because of the coming together of like letters, and then assimilated.

﴿Indeed, We have created everything﴾: the reading of the majority is *kulla shayʾin* in the accusative. Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative. Ibn ʿAtiyyah and a group of the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*, the orthodox majority) said: it is in the nominative. Abu al-Fath said: this is the correct reading in Arabic grammar (*al-ʿarabiyya*), and our reading in the accusative is with the community. Some said: when the verb may be taken as a descriptor, and what follows is suitable as a predicate, and the meaning is that the verb is the predicate, the accusative is chosen for the first noun so that it becomes clear that the verb is not a descriptor. This place is of that kind, because in the nominative reading one imagines that the verb is a descriptor and that a predicate must be supplied. The People of the Sunnah and the Qadariyyah have argued with this verse. The People of the Sunnah say: everything is created by God, the Exalted, by power; the proof is the accusative reading, because in such a construction only what can be a predicate if the first noun were the subject is explained. The Qadariyyah said: the reading in the nominative of *kullu* and *khalaqnāhu* is in the place of a descriptor of *kull*, meaning: if Our command or Our affair is everything We created, then it is according to measure or quantity, in the sense of its form, its time, and other than that. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*kulla shayʾin*" is in the accusative by a hidden verb that the apparent verb explains. It was also read as *kullu shayʾin* in the nominative. *Al-qadar* is measuring. It was also read with both, meaning: We created everything measured, firmly arranged, ordered according to what wisdom required, or measured and written in the Preserved Tablet, known before its existence, its state and time known to Us. End of quote. It was said: *al-qadar* has several meanings. The first: that it means quantity in its essence and attributes. The second: measuring, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿So We measured, and how excellent are the measurers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23]. A poet said:

*"And what the Merciful has measured is what is measured."*

That is, what is measured. The third: the *qadar* that is spoken of with *qaḍāʾ* (decree). It is said: that happened by the decree and measure of God. The meaning is that *qaḍāʾ* is what is in knowledge, and *qadar* is what is in will. So the meaning of the verse ﴿We created it by measure﴾ is: by power together with will. End of quote.

﴿And Our command is but one word﴾: that is, but one word, which is: "Be," and it is like a glance of the eye, a comparison to the swiftest thing perceived. Among things, the command of God, the Exalted, is more hidden than that. The meaning is that when He wills to bring a thing into being, it does not lag behind His will.

﴿And We have destroyed your likes﴾: that is, the sects that follow one another in a doctrine or religion.

﴿And everything they did﴾: that is, what the denying nations did is preserved against them until the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. The meaning of ﴿in the scriptures﴾ is: in the registers of the recording angels (*al-ḥafaẓa*).

﴿And every small and great﴾ matter among deeds, and among all that exists, ﴿is written down﴾: that is, recorded in the Tablet. It is said: *saṭṭartu* and *istaṭartu* have the same meaning. Al-Aʿmash, ʿImran ibn Hudayr, and ʿIsmah from Abu Bakr read *mustaṭarrun* with a doubled *rāʾ*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: it may be from *ṭarra* (to sprout), as with a plant or a moustache, when it appears and becomes firm, meaning: everything that is apparent in the Tablet and fixed in it. It may also be from *al-istiṭār* (to be written in lines), but the *rāʾ* was doubled for stopping (*waqf*), according to the dialect of those who say *jaʿfarr* and *nafʿallu* with doubling at pause. End of quote. Its form according to the first explanation is *istafʿala*, and according to the second *iftaʿala*. The majority read *wa-nahrin* in the singular with an open *hāʾ*. Al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, Humayd, Abu al-Sammal, and al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan read it with a sukun on the *hāʾ*. The intended meaning is the generic: if it means the rivers, or the meaning is abundance in provisions and dwellings. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*"I held her in my hand and widened her opening; one who stands beyond her can see what is behind her."*

That is: I widened her opening. Zuhayr al-ʿUqayli, al-Aʿmash, Abu Nahik, Abu Mijlaz, and al-Yamani read it with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and the *hāʾ*, as the plural of *nuhur*, like *rahn* and *ruhun*, or *nuhr* like *asad* and *usud*, which fits the plural *jannāt*. It was said that *nuhur* is the plural of *nahār* (day), and there is no night in Paradise, but this is far-fetched.

﴿In a seat of truth﴾: it may be the opposite of falsehood, meaning in the seat about which they spoke truly, and it may be from your saying "a man of truth," meaning of goodness, generosity, and righteousness. The majority read *fī maqʿadi* in the singular, intending the generic noun; ʿUthman al-Battiyy read *fī maqāʿida* in the plural. *ʿInda* (in the presence of) indicates nearness of rank to God, the Exalted. And God, the Exalted, knows best.

The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿The people of Lut denied the warnings.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind, except the family of Lut; We saved them at dawn,﴾ ﴿as a favor from Us. Thus do We reward those who give thanks.﴾ ﴿And he had warned them of Our assault, but they disputed the warnings.﴾ ﴿And they sought to seduce him from his guests, so We blinded their eyes: "Taste My punishment and warnings."﴾ ﴿And in the morning a settled punishment came upon them early.﴾ ﴿"So taste My punishment and warnings."﴾ ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance; so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿And the warnings certainly came to the family of Pharaoh.﴾ ﴿They denied all Our signs, so We seized them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Omnipotent.﴾ ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those? Or do you have immunity in the scriptures?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united company, victorious"?﴾ ﴿The company will be routed and they will turn their backs.﴾ ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and bitter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness.﴾ ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces: "Taste the touch of Saqar."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have created everything by measure.﴾ ﴿And Our command is but one word, like a glance of the eye.﴾ ﴿And We have destroyed your likes, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿And everything they did is in the scriptures.﴾ ﴿And every small and great matter is written down.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and rivers,﴾ ﴿in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent.﴾.

(p-182) The story of Lut, peace be upon him, and his people has already been related. The *ḥāṣib* (violent, pelting wind) derives from *al-ḥaṣbāʾ* (pebbles), and it is what is meant by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. ﴿Except the family of Lut﴾: it is said that this refers to his two daughters. ﴿At dawn (bi-saḥar)﴾: it means early morning, and for this reason it is given *tanwīn* (nunation, i.e., it takes the ending of an indefinite noun). ﴿A favor (niʿmatan)﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl min ajlihi*), meaning: We saved them because of Our bounty upon them; or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), because the meaning is: We bestowed a bounty by rescuing them. ﴿Thus do We reward﴾: that is, like that bounty and rescue, We reward ﴿those who give thanks﴾ for Our bounty, obey, and believe.

﴿And he had warned them of Our assault﴾: that is, Our seizing them with punishment. ﴿But they disputed﴾: that is, they doubted and engaged in that. ﴿The warnings﴾: that is, the admonition, or it may be the plural of *nadhīr* (warner).

﴿So We blinded﴾: Qatadah said: the blinding in reality was that Jibril, peace be upon him, drew his wing over their eyes, and their eyes became level with their faces. Abu ʿUbaydah said: their eyes were covered with a skin like a face. It was said: when Jibril struck them with his wing, he left them wandering, unable to find the door, until Lut, peace be upon him, brought them out. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said: this is a metaphor; He only veiled their perception, so they entered the house and saw nothing, and this was made like blinding. The majority read *fa-ṭamasnā* with a light *mīm*; Ibn Miqsam read it with a doubled *mīm*. ﴿Taste﴾: that is, I said to them through the tongues of the angels: "Taste."

﴿And in the morning He struck them early﴾: that is, at the beginning of the day and its earliest part, because of His words "shining" (*mushriqīn*) and "entering the morning" (*muṣbiḥīn*). The majority read *bukratan* with *tanwīn*, meaning *bukratan* from *al-bikr* (early), and so it takes the ending of an indefinite noun. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it without *tanwīn*.

﴿A settled punishment﴾: that is, no one removed it from them; rather, it continued with their death, then with what followed of the punishment of the grave, then the punishment of Hell.

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings﴾: this is emphasis and rebuke. The first was said at the blinding, and this at the morning arrival of the punishment. It was said: the purpose of repeating this and the repetition of ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy﴾ is to awaken the heart upon hearing each report from the reports of the former peoples, for admonition, and to renew alertness when they hear the urging toward that, lest heedlessness overtake them. The same is the rule for the repetition of ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 13] at each bounty enumerated in Surat al-Rahman, and the words ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 15] at each verse cited in Surat al-Mursalat. Likewise is the repetition of the stories in themselves, so that the lesson remains present in hearts and is mentioned at every time.

﴿And the warnings certainly came to the family of Pharaoh﴾: they are Musa, Harun, and other prophets, because the two of them presented to them what the messengers had warned of; or it may be the plural of *nadhīr* used as a verbal noun meaning warning. ﴿They denied Our signs﴾: these are the nine signs. The emphasis here is like that in His words: ﴿And We showed him all Our signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 56]. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿they denied﴾ and in ﴿so We seized them﴾ refers to the family of Pharaoh. It was also said that it refers to all the nations mentioned previously, and the speech is complete at the word ﴿the warnings﴾.

﴿So We seized them with the seizing of﴾ one who is ﴿Mighty﴾: unopposed; ﴿Omnipotent﴾: nothing can overcome Him.

﴿Are your disbelievers﴾: this is addressed to the people of Makkah. ﴿Better than those﴾: the reference is to the people of Nuh, Hud, Salih, and Lut, and to Pharaoh. The meaning is: are they better in strength, in the instruments of war, and in standing in this world, or less capable and more obstinate? Because they were not better, they are not exempt from punishment for disbelief in God. He placed them before a rebuke, meaning: your disbelievers are not better than those; rather, they are like them or worse than them, and you know what destruction befell those people, the complete uprooting, when they denied the messengers.

﴿Or do you have immunity in the scriptures﴾: that is, do you have in the divine books an immunity from the punishment of God, the Exalted? This was said by al-Dahhak, ʿIkrimah, and Ibn Zayd.

﴿Or do they say, "We are a united company﴾: that is, confident in our multitude, victorious by our strength, you say this out of self-admiration. The majority read *am yaqūlūna* with the third-person *yāʾ* (a shift to the third person), and likewise what follows, in the third person. Abu Haywah, Musa al-Aswari, and Abu al-Barahsam read it with the second-person *tāʾ* addressed to the disbelievers, following the address before it. They also read *sa-tahzimu al-jamʿa* with a *tāʾ* at the beginning, a *kasra* on the *zāy*, and a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*, addressed to the Messenger, ﷺ. Abu Haywah and Yaʿqub also read it with an open *nūn*, a *kasra* on the *zāy*, and a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*. The majority read it with a *yāʾ*, in the passive, with a *ḍamma* on the *ʿayn*. It was also reported from Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi ʿAbla: with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, in the active, and the *ʿayn* in the accusative, meaning: God will rout the company. The majority read *wa-yuwallūna* with the third-person *yāʾ*; Abu Haywah and Dawud ibn Abi Salim, from Abu ʿAmr, read it with the second-person *tāʾ*. Here *al-dubur* (the back) is a generic noun (*ism al-jins*). It occurs elsewhere as ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾ [al-Hashr: 12], which is the original form. The generic noun was made preferable here because it is the closing word of the verse (*fāṣila*). Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿and they will turn the back﴾, meaning *al-adbār* (the backs), as in the saying: "Eat in part of your belly so you will be chaste," and it was read as *al-adbār*. End of quote. But this is not like "your belly," because the singular *dubur* in this sense is not good, and the singular does not suit "your belly." In His words, the Exalted: ﴿The company will be routed﴾ is a promise from God to His Messenger, ﷺ, of the defeat of the company of Quraysh. The majority hold that the surah is Meccan, and the Messenger of God, ﷺ, recited it as evidence. It was also said that it was revealed on the day of Badr.

﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time﴾: he moved from those statements to the matter of the Hour, whose punishment is more severe for them than every defeat and battle.

﴿And the Hour is more calamitous﴾: that is, more terrible and more severe. *Al-dāhiya* is the bitterest calamity: the odious matter for which no way of repelling it is found; it is the great tragedy that befalls a person. ﴿Bitter (amarr)﴾ derives from *al-marāra* (bitterness); it is a metaphor for the difficulty of a thing upon the soul.

﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error﴾: that is, in confusion and turmoil in this world. ﴿And madness (suʿur)﴾: that is, burning in the Hereafter; they were placed in it because of their destination toward it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: and loss and madness; *al-suʿur* is madness, and something similar was mentioned in the story of Salih, peace be upon him.

﴿On the Day they are dragged﴾: they are pulled ﴿into the Fire﴾. In the reading of ʿAbdullah it is: ﴿into the Fire﴾ with *ilā*.

﴿Upon their faces, taste﴾: that is, it is said to them: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar.﴾ Mahbub, from Abu ʿAmr, read *massaqar* with the *sīn* assimilated into the *sīn*. Ibn Mujahid said: its assimilation is an error, because it is doubled. End of quote. But the presumption about Abu ʿAmr is that he did not assimilate until he deleted one of the two *sīns* because of the coming together of like letters, and then assimilated.

﴿Indeed, We have created everything﴾: the reading of the majority is *kulla shayʾin* in the accusative. Abu al-Sammal read it in the nominative. Ibn ʿAtiyyah and a group of the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*, the orthodox majority) said: it is in the nominative. Abu al-Fath said: this is the correct reading in Arabic grammar (*al-ʿarabiyya*), and our reading in the accusative is with the community. Some said: when the verb may be taken as a descriptor, and what follows is suitable as a predicate, and the meaning is that the verb is the predicate, the accusative is chosen for the first noun so that it becomes clear that the verb is not a descriptor. This place is of that kind, because in the nominative reading one imagines that the verb is a descriptor and that a predicate must be supplied. The People of the Sunnah and the Qadariyyah have argued with this verse. The People of the Sunnah say: everything is created by God, the Exalted, by power; the proof is the accusative reading, because in such a construction only what can be a predicate if the first noun were the subject is explained. The Qadariyyah said: the reading in the nominative of *kullu* and *khalaqnāhu* is in the place of a descriptor of *kull*, meaning: if Our command or Our affair is everything We created, then it is according to measure or quantity, in the sense of its form, its time, and other than that. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*kulla shayʾin*" is in the accusative by a hidden verb that the apparent verb explains. It was also read as *kullu shayʾin* in the nominative. *Al-qadar* is measuring. It was also read with both, meaning: We created everything measured, firmly arranged, ordered according to what wisdom required, or measured and written in the Preserved Tablet, known before its existence, its state and time known to Us. End of quote. It was said: *al-qadar* has several meanings. The first: that it means quantity in its essence and attributes. The second: measuring, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿So We measured, and how excellent are the measurers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23]. A poet said:

*"And what the Merciful has measured is what is measured."*

That is, what is measured. The third: the *qadar* that is spoken of with *qaḍāʾ* (decree). It is said: that happened by the decree and measure of God. The meaning is that *qaḍāʾ* is what is in knowledge, and *qadar* is what is in will. So the meaning of the verse ﴿We created it by measure﴾ is: by power together with will. End of quote.

﴿And Our command is but one word﴾: that is, but one word, which is: "Be," and it is like a glance of the eye, a comparison to the swiftest thing perceived. Among things, the command of God, the Exalted, is more hidden than that. The meaning is that when He wills to bring a thing into being, it does not lag behind His will.

﴿And We have destroyed your likes﴾: that is, the sects that follow one another in a doctrine or religion.

﴿And everything they did﴾: that is, what the denying nations did is preserved against them until the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. The meaning of ﴿in the scriptures﴾ is: in the registers of the recording angels (*al-ḥafaẓa*).

﴿And every small and great﴾ matter among deeds, and among all that exists, ﴿is written down﴾: that is, recorded in the Tablet. It is said: *saṭṭartu* and *istaṭartu* have the same meaning. Al-Aʿmash, ʿImran ibn Hudayr, and ʿIsmah from Abu Bakr read *mustaṭarrun* with a doubled *rāʾ*. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: it may be from *ṭarra* (to sprout), as with a plant or a moustache, when it appears and becomes firm, meaning: everything that is apparent in the Tablet and fixed in it. It may also be from *al-istiṭār* (to be written in lines), but the *rāʾ* was doubled for stopping (*waqf*), according to the dialect of those who say *jaʿfarr* and *nafʿallu* with doubling at pause. End of quote. Its form according to the first explanation is *istafʿala*, and according to the second *iftaʿala*. The majority read *wa-nahrin* in the singular with an open *hāʾ*. Al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, Humayd, Abu al-Sammal, and al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan read it with a sukun on the *hāʾ*. The intended meaning is the generic: if it means the rivers, or the meaning is abundance in provisions and dwellings. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

*"I held her in my hand and widened her opening; one who stands beyond her can see what is behind her."*

That is: I widened her opening. Zuhayr al-ʿUqayli, al-Aʿmash, Abu Nahik, Abu Mijlaz, and al-Yamani read it with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and the *hāʾ*, as the plural of *nuhur*, like *rahn* and *ruhun*, or *nuhr* like *asad* and *usud*, which fits the plural *jannāt*. It was said that *nuhur* is the plural of *nahār* (day), and there is no night in Paradise, but this is far-fetched.

﴿In a seat of truth﴾: it may be the opposite of falsehood, meaning in the seat about which they spoke truly, and it may be from your saying "a man of truth," meaning of goodness, generosity, and righteousness. The majority read *fī maqʿadi* in the singular, intending the generic noun; ʿUthman al-Battiyy read *fī maqāʿida* in the plural. *ʿInda* (in the presence of) indicates nearness of rank to God, the Exalted. And God, the Exalted, knows best.
